# guluswm

<!-- badges: start -->

[![License: CC BY
4.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-CC_BY_4.0-lightgrey.svg)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/openwashdata/guluswm/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/openwashdata/guluswm/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)

<!-- badges: end -->

The goal of guluswm is to provide the field data of a household solid
waste study in Gulu City, northern Uganda, as tidy data. The study
combined a socio-economic household survey of 424 households in six areas
of the city's two divisions, conducted face to face with the mWater
platform from 23 to 26 September 2026, with a seven day waste
characterisation study in which the waste of 95 households was weighed and
sorted into 16 fractions on 1 to 3 October 2026. The data were collected
by Ivan Feni, Abubakar Batte, James Omal, Charles Wakhata (logistics,
support to the enumeration and the waste characterisation), the
enumerators Juliet Amindre, Alex Candia, Rebecca Lamwaka and Grace Okello,
and Charles B. Niwagaba, of Makerere University, the University of
Stuttgart and Gulu City Council, for a manuscript in preparation, and shared with openwashdata for publication
under the CC BY 4.0 licence. The fieldwork was funded by Integers Company
Limited. Ivan Feni is the contact for questions about the data.

**Draft.** This package is not released and has no DOI. The open
questions on the data went to the authors on 30 October 2026, and they
answered on 2 November 2026 with a corrected export of the workbook, the
wealth index and the survey weights, and sent the final copy of the
workbook with coded enumerators on 3 November 2026 (corrected the same
day), which is archived in `data-raw/`.

## Installation

You can install the development version of guluswm from
[GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("openwashdata/guluswm")
```

```{r}
## Run the following code in console if you don't have the packages
## install.packages(c("dplyr", "knitr", "readr", "stringr", "gt", "kableExtra"))
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)
library(kableExtra)
```

Alternatively, you can download the individual datasets as a CSV or XLSX
file from the table below.

1.  Click Download CSV. A window opens that displays the CSV in
    your browser.
2.  Right-click anywhere inside the window and select "Save Page As...".
3.  Save the file in a folder of your choice.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

extdata_path <- "https://github.com/openwashdata/guluswm/raw/main/inst/extdata/"

read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |> 
  distinct(file_name) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(file_name = str_remove(file_name, ".rda")) |> 
  dplyr::rename(dataset = file_name) |> 
  mutate(
    CSV = paste0("[Download CSV](", extdata_path, dataset, ".csv)"),
    XLSX = paste0("[Download XLSX](", extdata_path, dataset, ".xlsx)")
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable()

```

## Data

The package provides access to two data objects. `guluswm_survey` holds
one row per household interviewed in the household survey, and
`guluswm_waste` one row per household in the waste characterisation
study. The two studies were run by separate field teams in the same six
areas, and their households cannot be linked.

```{r}
library(guluswm)
```

### guluswm_survey

The dataset `guluswm_survey` contains data about the interviewed
households: household size, the education and livelihood of the household
head, income and expenditure bands, housing and utilities, the types of
waste generated, how waste is stored and disposed of, who collects it, how
the collection service is rated, whether the household pays for
collection and how much, whether it is willing to pay for an improved
service and at what amount, and its awareness of by-laws. It has
`r nrow(guluswm_survey)` observations and `r ncol(guluswm_survey)`
variables

```{r}
guluswm_survey |> 
  head(3) |> 
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::as_raw_html()
```

For an overview of the variable names, see the following table.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
readr::read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(file_name == "guluswm_survey.rda") |>
  dplyr::select(variable_name:description) |> 
  knitr::kable() |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling("striped") |> 
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

### guluswm_waste

The dataset `guluswm_waste` contains data about the waste each household
stored over seven consecutive days: the number of occupants, the total
weight as recorded and as used in the analysis, the per capita generation
rate, the bulk density measured with a 10 litre bucket, and the weight of
each of the 16 sorted fractions before and after the deduction of the
container weight. It has `r nrow(guluswm_waste)` observations and
`r ncol(guluswm_waste)` variables

```{r}
guluswm_waste |> 
  head(3) |> 
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::as_raw_html()
```

For an overview of the variable names, see the following table.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
readr::read_csv("data-raw/dictionary.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(file_name == "guluswm_waste.rda") |>
  dplyr::select(variable_name:description) |> 
  knitr::kable() |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling("striped") |> 
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

## Example

The figure `generation-by-area` shows the per capita waste generation
rate of the 94 households included in the study's averages, one point per
household, grouped by study area and ordered by the median of the area.
Generation differs between areas more than between the two divisions, and
in every area a few households generate far more than the rest.

```{r generation-by-area, fig.alt="Dot plot of the per capita waste generation rate in kilograms per person and day for 94 households, one row per study area ordered by median, with the median of each area marked"}
library(guluswm)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(2026)
analysed <- guluswm_waste |>
  filter(included_in_averages == "Yes") |>
  mutate(area = reorder(area, generation_kg_cap_day, FUN = median))

medians <- analysed |>
  group_by(area, division) |>
  summarise(median = median(generation_kg_cap_day), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(analysed, aes(x = generation_kg_cap_day, y = area)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = division), height = 0.15, alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = medians, aes(x = median), shape = 124, size = 8) +
  geom_text(data = medians, aes(x = 1.45, label = paste0("n = ", n)),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.6), breaks = seq(0, 1.5, 0.25)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Bardege-Layibi` = "#B5473B",
                                 `Laroo-Pece` = "#5B8E7D")) +
  labs(x = "Waste generation (kg per person and day)", y = NULL,
       colour = "Division",
       title = "Household waste generation by study area, Gulu City, 2026",
       subtitle = "One point per household; the bar marks the median of the area") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Source and changes

The data come from the field data workbook of the Gulu City household
solid waste study, shared by its authors with openwashdata in October
2026, re-exported by them with corrections and sent as a final copy
without personal data on 3 November 2026
(`data-raw/Gulu_SWM_OpenWashData_final.xlsx`). The study is described in Feni, I., Batte, A., Omal, J. and
Niwagaba, C. B., *Household waste generation, composition and willingness
to pay for collection in Gulu City, Uganda: implications for user charges
in secondary cities* (manuscript in preparation). The household survey
was administered in English or Acholi by five trained enumerators after
verbal consent; the waste characterisation followed the sorting
categories of ASTM D5231, with polyethylene bags and inert fines (sand,
soil and stones from compound sweeping) recorded as separate fractions.

We changed the material. The two sheets of the workbook were read into R
(the script is in `data-raw/data_processing.R`), the column names were
rewritten in snake case with the unit in the name where there is one, the
ordered categories became factors in the order of the questionnaire, and
the survey sheet's spelling "Pabwo Quarters" was aligned with "Pabbo
Quarters" as used in the characterisation sheet and the manuscript.
Multi-answer questions stay as one string with the answers separated by a
semicolon, as in the workbook. The survey weight by division and the
wealth index score and class, which the authors computed and sent
separately, were added to the survey table by household ID. At the
authors' decision, three groups of columns are not published: the
household coordinates of both sheets (the survey consent did not cover
household locations), the identifiers that carry an enumerator's name
(the enumerator is kept as a code E1 to E5, also in the household ID,
where it replaces the enumerator's initials), and the three free text
answers of the survey, whose coded versions are included. The script
`analysis/validate_data.R` recomputes the figures of the manuscript from
the data objects.
